1.pericope_label: The burden of the word of the Lord for Israel, saith the Lord, which stretcheth forth the heavens, and layeth the foundation of the earth, and formeth the spirit of man within him. Behold, I will make Jerusalem a cup of trembling unto all the people round about, when they shall be in the siege both against Judah and against Jerusalem. And in that day will I make Jerusalem a burdensome stone for all people: all that burden themselves with it shall be cut in pieces, though all the people of the earth be gathered together against it.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch supply the frame, this being the first half of a second prophecy on the judgment by which the people of God are refined and sifted through conflict with the nations, and they make the vessel of the second verse a reeling-basin, the word meaning here not threshold but a large bowl. Ellicott settles the name Israel lexically, the several names used in the preceding chapters having been interchangeable after the captivity, and on the burdensome stone prefers a building stone that lacerates those who would work it into the fabric of their own dominion, allowing also the athletic sense and the general one of a weight too heavy to be borne.

Gill takes the burden as for Israel and against their enemies, for the joy and salvation of the church, allowing also the sense concerning them; on the stone he reports the custom, attested by an ancient writer for the towns of Palestine and for a brazen globe at Athens, of youths lifting a great round stone to try their strength. Calvin alone finds the title at odds with the chapter, since the word is rightly taken for a threatening prophecy yet no evil is denounced on the chosen people here, and answers that the threat falls on the Israelites who preferred exile to God's favour and were not gathered again when the return was freely offered.

Clarke calls it a new prophecy directed to both kingdoms though only one is named, refers the first part to an invasion in the latter ages of the world, takes one inference from the third clause of the opening title, that the spirit is not the same substance with the body, and thinks the burdensome stone the weight laid on the breast of a man condemned to die, which broke the whole chest. Wesley applies the cup past the city to the church, its antitype, and keeps to the plainest sense of the stone, that it is too heavy though they all join to remove it.

Henry keeps the burden double-edged, heavy to the church's enemies but comfort to Israel, as the pillar in the wilderness turned a bright side to one camp and a black side to the other. He takes the three clauses of the divine title in order, the heavens kept stretched like a curtain, the earth kept firm though hung upon nothing, and the spirit formed within man still, the body from the fathers of our flesh but the soul infused by the Father of spirits, whence he draws that God can save his church by inspiriting its friends and dispiriting its foes.

debates.question: Does the word burden in the title suit a chapter that denounces no evil on God's people?

positions.position: No, and the difficulty is real: the threat must fall on the Israelites who refused to return, or the chapter has no meaning.
It does: the same word is a burden to the church's enemies and a comfort to Israel at once.
No difficulty arises; the title simply announces a new prophecy for Israel and against their enemies.

debates.question: What is the figure behind the burdensome stone?

positions.position: The weight laid on the breast of a man condemned to be stoned, which broke the whole chest.
A great round stone lifted by youths to try their strength, a custom attested in Palestine and Greece.
A building stone that lacerates those who try to work it into their own fabric, though the athletic and the general senses are allowed.
Simply a weight too heavy to be moved, which breaks those who burden themselves with it.

outliers.claim: Charges the interpreters with passing heedlessly over the force of the title, and holds that the grief threatened belongs to the ten tribes, who through their own sloth were not gathered again and must see their brethren protected while they themselves are without hope.

themes: The burden of the word of the Lord for Israel, saith the Lord, which stretcheth forth the heavens, and layeth the foundation of the earth, and formeth the spirit of man within him.
Behold, I will make Jerusalem a cup of trembling unto all the people round about, when they shall be in the siege both against Judah and against Jerusalem.
And in that day will I make Jerusalem a burdensome stone for all people: all that burden themselves with it shall be cut in pieces, though all the people of the earth be gathered together against it.

4.pericope_label: In that day, saith the Lord, I will smite every horse with astonishment, and his rider with madness: and I will open mine eyes upon the house of Judah, and will smite every horse of the people with blindness. And the governors of Judah shall say in their heart, The inhabitants of Jerusalem shall be my strength in the Lord of hosts their God. In that day will I make the governors of Judah like an hearth of fire among the wood, and like a torch of fire in a sheaf; and they shall devour all the people round about, on the right hand and on the left: and Jerusalem shall be inhabited again in her own place, even in Jerusalem. The Lord also shall save the tents of Judah first, that the glory of the house of David and the glory of the inhabitants of Jerusalem do not magnify themselves against Judah. In that day shall the Lord defend the inhabitants of Jerusalem; and he that is feeble among them at that day shall be as David; and the house of David shall be as God, as the angel of the Lord before them.

schools.summary: Ellicott takes the deliverance of Judah before Jerusalem to mean the people at large as against the capital and the princes, since the Maccabean deliverers were raised up from the people and not the royal house, and finds the promise about the feeble fulfilled in the aged father who began that struggle; he corrects a tense in the fifth verse, reading are rather than shall be, records a rival reading of the word first supported by the ancient Greek and a few manuscripts, and corrects one word of the received version to nations. Keil and Delitzsch render the run of promises without comment.

Gill looks forward to armies of his own century whose cavalry he thinks may be in view in the smiting of horse and rider, takes the madness for enemies astonished at their failure and filled with fury, has the outlying governors take heart at what is done to the horses, and reads the tents of Judah as Jews encamped outside the city and saved first, so that the salvation may appear the Lord's.

Clarke reports and rejects the Maccabean application of the smiting, the terms being too strong for victories so petty and evanescent, infers from the phrase about the governors a union between the two kingdoms, reads the promise of rebuilding as a future conversion and return, and turns the saving of the tents first into a gospel principle, that eminent men are not the first called and the poor have good tidings preached to them. Wesley reads the opened eyes as a watching over God's people for good and the blindness as want of foresight in the enemy's counsels, glosses the hearth as one thoroughly kindled, insists that the city will stand on the very same ground, and calls the promise about the feeble a hyperbole.

Henry presses the military detail, that horses and horsemen alike forget the exercise they were trained to and break their ranks so that the church's infantry proves too hard for the enemy's cavalry; he guards the hearth against being read as fury, since Zion's King is meek and lowly and it is God's wrath that burns, the enemies who thought to be water to that fire being made wood and then a sheaf; and he insists that the natives will not settle a colony elsewhere and call it Jerusalem, carrying the promise on to the gospel church, which may call every place its own.

debates.question: Do these promises refer to the Maccabean wars?

positions.position: No: the terms are too strong for victories so petty and evanescent, and the prophecy is likelier not yet accomplished.
Yes, twice over: the deliverers were raised up from the people rather than the royal house, and the aged father who began the struggle fulfils the promise about the feeble.
The reference is to armies of a later age altogether.

debates.question: Why are the tents of Judah saved before Jerusalem?

positions.position: So that the salvation may plainly appear to be the Lord's.
The weaker are saved before the stronger, the unfenced places and cottages first.
As a gospel principle, that no secular influence may appear in the matter.
The word first may instead be read as in former times, on a variant that does not materially alter the sense.

outliers.claim: The natives of Jerusalem will not incorporate a colony in another country and call it Jerusalem and see the promises fulfilled in that, as English settlers named their new towns after the towns they had left.

9.pericope_label: And it shall come to pass in that day, that I will seek to destroy all the nations that come against Jerusalem. And I will pour upon the house of David, and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the spirit of grace and of supplications: and they shall look upon me whom they have pierced, and they shall mourn for him, as one mourneth for his only son, and shall be in bitterness for him, as one that is in bitterness for his firstborn. In that day shall there be a great mourning in Jerusalem, as the mourning of Hadadrimmon in the valley of Megiddon. And the land shall mourn, every family apart; the family of the house of David apart, and their wives apart; the family of the house of Nathan apart, and their wives apart; The family of the house of Levi apart, and their wives apart; the family of Shimei apart, and their wives apart; All the families that remain, every family apart, and their wives apart.

schools.summary: Ellicott observes that the verb rendered seek is used of God only twice, and takes the sense from the other place, that God expressed a determination he did not carry out, so that here too he would have destroyed the nations utterly but for his people's own sin. On the mourning he quotes an ancient writer for a city near Jezreel, notes that specialists in Assyrian pronounce the name differently, and answers the objection that the phrase is a note of time fixing the prophecy shortly after that king's death; he also identifies the two lesser families named, the first not the prophet of that name but a son of the king, the second not the Benjamite but of the house of Gershon. Keil and Delitzsch put the renewal in a sentence and place the same city near Jerusalem instead.
Gill reads the house of David as the family of Christ and grounds the mourning of the priestly tribe in their contempt of his priestly office.

Clarke sets the destruction of the nations far off, at a time when the longsuffering of God shall wait no longer, lays out four steps by which the nation is brought in — the spirit of grace, continual prayer, Christ preached, and a deep repentance — and takes the separation of the families for the depth of the sorrow, each avoiding the rest to vent his grief in private. Wesley reads the same verb as force rather than reservation, dates the outpouring from the exaltation of Christ and the sending of the Comforter, says every one of us pierced him by our sins and many of the Jews literally, and presses hardest on the priestly tribe, whose head condemned Christ to die.

Henry holds that the seeking implies no want of means, since Infinite Wisdom was never at a loss, but earnestness, God overruling every instrument to that end. He makes prayer the hinge, that when God intends great mercy the first thing he does is set his people praying, so that he destroys their enemies by stirring them to ask it. On the piercing he says it is spoken primarily of those who persecuted him to death yet is true of us all, and makes the looking and the mourning inseparable; and he gives the reason for naming families at all, that all have contributed to the guilt and all shall share the grief.

debates.question: What force has the verb rendered seek when used of God?

positions.position: A determination expressed but not carried out: God would have destroyed the nations utterly but for his people's sin.
Full force: God will purposely and effectually do it.
Neither reservation nor mere force but earnestness, since no want of means can be supposed in Infinite Wisdom.

debates.question: Where was the place whose mourning is the comparison?

positions.position: A city near Jerusalem, afterwards renamed, in the field of Megiddo.
A city near Jezreel, on the same ancient authority.

outliers.claim: That a town in that tribe already bore an Assyrian name in the prophet's own day is near proof that the prophecy belongs to the period after the exile, the mourning for the slain king having become an ordinance rather than serving as a note of time.
